Wouldn't you rather participate in space development than just read about the speculations of big corporations and space agencies? Wouldn't you rather do stuff than just sit around waiting for Elon Musk's mothership to land? It's very good that companies like Lockheed are finally taking the concept of telerobotics seriously and realizing how it can be leveraged on facilitating the pre-development of infrastructures to increase the safety and feasibility of later human activity. But there's something they've overlooked about this. There's a lot of development and design work that needs to be done to optimize the potential use of telerobots in space. A lot of things we need to figure out how to do with such machines. And most of that work doesn't actually require the facilities of space agencies and giant corporations to do. Truth-be-told, the level of sophistication of space robotics isn't all that higher than that of amateur robotics. Kids in Japan are doing things with robots in their own homes that aren't that far behind what's being done at NASA right now. The chief difference is in the resilience of parts and materials they get to work with, which only really matters when you're ready to actually deploy hardware in space. There's enough fundamental work to do before that point to keep millions of people busy before they ever actually need such advanced hardware. And that means that this is an area of development where regular folks working with cheap and hacked hardware could actually participate, contribute, and innovate if they had a model of activity to rally around.

Last year the ESA announced their latest moonbase concept showcasing a moonbase design by Fosters and Partners. Jumping on the current 3D printed architecture craze, the concept features the telerobotic construction of a habitat structures based on the use of an inflatable shell serving as formwork for a rigid shell 3D printed from regolith by a pair of small robots over a period of about 6 months. Though Fosters touts this as some cutting edge technology, it's actually a derivative of a very old, simple, building concept that was once used by the German military in WWII to construct bunkers and underground aircraft hangers. Known as 'mound-formed shell construction' is based on the use of piled-up mounds of gravel as forms over which one assembles a rebar mesh then layers a relatively dry concrete mix to form a rigid shell. When the shell is cured, it is covered in earth for added protection and the gravel is excavated out of the hollow space to be reused for making additional structures. One nice example of architecture based on that that I often point to as an analog to space settlements is Grin Grin Park in Fukuoka Japan. Many variations on this concept have been proposed for space habitat use since the 1960s.

The simplicity of this technique makes it well suited to telerobotic use and the use of relatively crude locally sourced materials. If you have a shell material that can be built-up relatively slowly, you can take all the time you want and divide the labor into small volumes of material. This is why they can propose doing this with just a pair of small robots. But you don't even need that to demonstrate this construction process on Earth. We can create a full scale mock-up of such a habitat right now using toys!

Though less popular in the US where racing tends to dominate, in Europe there's a popular segment of the RC model hobby involving construction vehicles; excavators, bulldozers, dump trucks, semis, wheel loaders, farm vehicles, forklifts and container handlers, cranes, on and on. And the folks in this hobby aren't just interested in realism of appearance. They're interested in realism of function. So these have become quite sophisticated robots in their own right, with all sorts of working features, some with powerful mini-hydraulics, first-person video systems, and sophisticated digital control. And all around the year, all over Europe, there are meets and shows where they setup miniature villages in which these machines can be put through their paces, moving real earth, building landscape features, transporting cargo around, all done cooperatively like the traditional community model train layout. You could build real stuff with these machines--although it would take a while. On Youtube a US farmer who was into these models documented his use of them to expand his home's basement, turning the space into a miniature construction zone as he used the machines to slowly excavate the basement extension in his spare time. The 1/8th scale models are quite powerful and are roughly the same size as the robots Fosters proposes for building their moonbase.

Even in professional robotics, there's a well established tradition of repurposing the components from RC modeling for robot development because robotics, generally, doesn't yet have a real industrial ecology of its own. It's still in the 'mainframe' era where things are based largely on repurposing components from other industries. This, in particular, is what gave us the multirotor drone so popular today. Originally, these were created with RC plane components and inertial sensors scavenged from Nintendo WII controllers. And now the drone is the first class of personal robots with an actual international industrial ecology like that of the PC. With more purpose-designed amateur robots, one could demonstrate this construction process more efficiently and realistically and these RC models offer a good source of hackable components toward that end. Ideally, you would want a control platform to let you manage this construction process over the internet. This is completely feasible at a modest cost, and potentially a lot of fun and very appealing to the public. Yet the ESA itself has done absolutely nothing to demonstrate this.

I think it's time to create an amateur space program to do this. An overlooked bit of computer history is that the concept of 'hacking', along with many principles of modern computing and digital systems control, originated in MIT's Tech Model Railway Club and their community model train layout built in a disused campus building. This exists to this day, still serving as a useful petri dish for systems control theory and a good creative outlet for the students and faculty. But now we have the internet to let people all over the world participate. It's not stuck secluded behind the space center fence. And there are an endless assortment of locations, structures, building techniques each with their own unique logistics to explore. I think mockup telerobotic bases--telebases--could be the new TMRC.
